faqs.q: Bats are in our downtown Sanford building — when can they be excluded?
faqs.a: In Florida's legal window only: August 15 through April 15. Sanford's older commercial buildings host free-tailed and evening bat colonies that maternity-season law protects from April 16 to August 14 — during those months we survey at dusk, identify and count the colony, seal the unused openings, and stage the exclusion for the first legal week. A colony excluded out of season is both illegal and counterproductive, since trapped pups die inside and create a worse problem than the bats.

Sanford.wildlife_intro:
Sanford sits on Lake Monroe's south shore — a historic brick downtown, the St. Johns River running north from the lake, and the Celery City's farming heritage in the fields east and south. River-and-lake wildlife leads: raccoons and opossums in the historic homes, roof rats downtown and in the older neighborhoods, armadillos in the sandy yards, and along the river and in the Geneva woods east, deer, hogs at the field edges, and the occasional bear report routed to FWC. The riverfront marina adds dock work.

Sanford service splits historic and modern as the town does: brick-district carpentry and bat surveys for the old buildings, subdivision packages for the Lake Mary-border growth, and farm walks for the celery-field acreage. Hog sign at a property's wild edge gets an honest referral to specialist trappers. Downtown's bat colonies follow the legal season — out by April 15 or booked for after August 15 — and our inspections say which side of the line a colony falls on before quoting.

faqs.q: Why are roof rats such a problem in Altamonte Springs?
faqs.a: Roof rats are Florida's main structure rat, and Altamonte Springs gives them exactly what they want: palm crowns, fruit trees, dense shrubs, and rooflines they can reach from fences and branches. They nest in attics and wall voids and breed year-round here. Our crew traps and excludes — sealing the entry and cutting back roof access — and frames structure work as nonchemical trapping and exclusion, because chemical rodent work in a structure is FDACS Chapter 482 pest-control territory.

In Altamonte Springs, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — dense Orlando suburbs, lakefront towns, and river and spring corridors — and features such as St. Johns River, Lake Monroe, Wekiva River, Little Big Econ State Forest keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Altamonte Springs jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Oviedo?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Oviedo. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.

faqs.q: Lake Jesup is known for alligators — what does that mean for our neighborhood?
faqs.a: Vigilance at the waterline, and nothing more dramatic. Lake Jesup's gators are FWC-managed residents; the nuisance program responds to animals four feet or longer that threaten people, pets, or property, sending its own trappers. For lakeside homeowners the rules are eternal: never feed a gator, keep dogs leashed and out of the shallows at dawn and dusk, and supervise the bank. Your roofline wildlife — squirrels, rats, raccoons — is where a private company's work actually lives, and ours is quoted after inspection.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Longwood?
faqs.a: Longwood figures weigh canopy density honestly: heavy-contact homes carry more sealing points and a trimming component, quoted together in writing after the limb map is drawn.

faqs.q: Why does Longwood have so many attic squirrels?
faqs.a: Because Longwood is a hammock with streets. The continuous oak and palm canopy lets gray squirrels travel the whole city overhead, the acorn and palm-fruit crops feed two litters a year, and the older housing stock offers eaves that soften a little more each decade. The durable answer is the one we quote: remove the current tenants, seal every entry with metal-backed materials, and cut the limb bridges back beyond jumping range. Trapping alone in Longwood is a revolving door with a fee attached.

Longwood.wildlife_intro:
Longwood is Seminole County's historic small city — the Bradlee-McIntyre house and the old district under moss-draped oaks, Big Tree Park's ancient cypress (the Senator's surviving neighbors) nearby, and subdivisions woven between lakes and the Wekiva River's approach. Canopy and water in equal measure: squirrels and raccoons in the historic homes, roof rats near the lakes, bats in the old rooflines, and armadillos in the deep-shade yards where grubs thrive in the leaf litter.

Longwood work is shade-country craft: the inspections map limb contact first, because in this canopy the roof is a branch terminus. Historic homes get fitted eave work. The Wekiva-edge properties get bear-aware trash counsel — this is bear corridor county, and FWC's program is the referral. Our trapping follows the county standard: daily checks, releases on site or in-county on permitted 40-acre ground, and sealing as the durable half of every job.
